Edinburgh Castle is a historic fortress which dominates the skyline of the city of Edinburgh, Scotland, from its position on the Castle Rock. Archaeologists have established human occupation of the rock since at least the Iron Age (2nd century AD), although the nature of the early settlement is unclear. There has been a royal castle on the rock since at least the reign of David I in the 12th century, and the site continued to be a royal residence until the Union of the Crowns in 1603. From the 15th century the castle's residential role declined, and by the 17th century it was principally used as military barracks with a large garrison. Its importance as a part of Scotland's national heritage was recognised increasingly from the early 19th century onwards, and various restoration programmes have been carried out over the past century and a half. As one of the most important strongholds in the Kingdom of Scotland, Edinburgh Castle was involved in many historical conflicts from the Wars of Scottish Independence in the 14th century to the Jacobite Rising of 1745. Research undertaken in 2014 identified 26 sieges in its 1100-year-old history, giving it a claim to having been "the most besieged place in Great Britain and one of the most attacked in the world".

This idea has actually turned up often in the space advocacy community over the years. Space advocacy is always looking for a way to catalyze the focus of society at large toward the goals of space development and it seems as though religions very easily manage to coerce huge amounts of attention, money, creativity, and productivity out of society on the most ridiculous premises. If you're willing to compromise your scruples for the sake of what you think is a greater good, creating a space religion to coerce society into supporting a space program would seem clever.

But in practice, the sort of gullible people who are likely to adopt a young made-up religion are not the sort of people able to engage in concerted science and engineering work. You would somehow need to cultivate a community of dupes devotees as a cash cow and keep it isolated from the working community of scientists and engineers, trusting that they too generally share your same lack of scruples about exploiting religiosity for the sake of their jobs. Cultivating a religion actually has a pretty high overhead. You have to spend a lot of money on the 'show' maintaining your followers. That overhead would constantly compete with your investment in actual space development. Alien contactee cults like the Raelians do seem to engage in science work. They are known for their obsession with genetics and cloning and have sponsored the creation of research institutes and key scientists. But their results are pretty poor. The 'scientists' they recruit and the work they engage in are rather dubious. Always, the compulsion to greed overcomes the leadership of such religions and any higher mission--if there is one--is soon forgotten.

A similar notion of faking alien contact also often turns up in space advocacy. The idea is that society would be more willing to support a space program if they believed there was actual alien life out there for us to go visit. So one might catalyze this by carefully faking evidence of aliens, such as a radio signal from space. This idea may originate in the plot of an old Outer Limits TV episode called The Architects of Fear where a member of a secret organization seeking to save the world from a Cold War apocalypse subjects one of its members to a horrific surgical transformation so he can pose as an alien invader making a false-flag attack in order to scare the world into global unity to defend against the cosmic threat.

As former president of a space advocacy organization, I long suggested that cultivating community was key to catalyzing space development as a mass cultural imperative. So I sought to develop intentional communities--high-tech eco-villages--offering a lifestyle supportive to space science and engineering careers and that could evolve into a Vienna of space. A New Zvyozdny Gorodok--Star City. A planned city that could be a locus of commercial space activity where the goals of space development were as fundamental to the local culture as music and the arts are to the culture of Vienna. Because we aren't going to be moving out into space if our only imperative is economic. Economic logic is about to replace us all with robots in the offices and factories right here on Earth, so we're most-certainly going to soon be obsolete in space as well. If we want to live in space, it's a lifestyle choice that must be supported by other means/reasons than economic, otherwise the only people with the option will be a few oligarchs.

Unfortunately, space advocacy has so terribly deteriorated intellectually and philosophically that such a notion proved completely incomprehensible to the community. It was like suggesting cathedral-building to people who think Salvage 1 was a documentary. Sadly, I've come to the conclusion that our contemporary efforts in space may be all prove futile because of this. We have probably already ceded the stars to our electric children; the AIs and artilects of the near future. But I still think there's much public participation possible now, particularly through amateur telerobotics. I think the creation of prototype telebases as online equivalents of community model train layouts could go a long way toward opening real space development activity to participation by a large global community. But, again, it's not something that fits people's typical SciFi fantasies of space adventure, so no one gets it.
